alalal-e93544-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 7: whether it is true, as Gregory's exposition says, that John the Baptist doubted Christ's descent into hell.

alalal-e93544-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's text about those who take John the Baptist as evidence on this point.

alalal-e93544-d1e129.summary: States that this opinion seems heretical.

alalal-e93544-d1e137.summary: First reason: the descent into hell is expressed in the creed in the article Thomas contributed, 'he descended into hell, on the third day he rose'.

alalal-e93544-d1e151.summary: Second: Anselm says in De processione Spiritus sancti that belief in the descent into hell is necessary for salvation.

alalal-e93544-d1e165.summary: Third: all expositors but Gregory agree that John did not doubt for himself but acted for his disciples, who envied and doubted Christ; Christ answered nothing about descending himself or through another but showed proofs of his divinity; and in John's Gospel John persuades his disciples that he must decrease and Christ increase.

alalal-e93544-d1e202.summary: Solution: it is rash to say that John doubted, and the beginning of the Manichaean heresy, which says he doubted and was therefore damned. Albert excuses Gregory: John could have 'doubted' the mode of the descent for the sake of his disciples, not for himself, and so, about to die, he sent his disciples, rivals of Christ, to be confounded by what they saw and adhere to Christ.
claims: John the Baptist did not doubt Christ's descent for himself; his question was for his disciples' sake.

alalal-e93544.summary: Article 7 examines Gregory's exposition that John the Baptist doubted whether Christ would descend into hell himself. The descent is in the creed, Anselm calls belief in it necessary, and all other expositors say John asked on behalf of his disciples. Albert judges it rash, and the beginning of the Manichaean heresy that John was damned, to say John doubted. He excuses Gregory by reading the doubt as concerning the mode of the descent and as raised for his disciples' sake: John sent his envious disciples to Christ so that what they saw would make them adhere to him.
claims: John the Baptist did not doubt Christ's descent into hell for himself.
Saying that John doubted is rash and leads toward the Manichaean error.
